title: Fiction Writing: Craft & Style
description: Advanced fiction craft — descriptive writing, linguistic devices for effect, sentence control for tension, structure for effect, and narrative voice.

notes.heading: Precision: Upgrading Nouns, Verbs and Adjectives
notes.body: In Creative Writing (eng-creative-1) you learned to build scenes with sensory detail; the next step is word-level precision. Weak description relies on vague words propped up by adverbs — 'the man walked quickly into the big room'. Upgrade the verb and the adverb becomes unnecessary: 'strode', 'shuffled', 'crept' each tell the reader HOW he moved and hint at WHY. Upgrade the noun too: not 'a bird' but 'a kestrel'; not 'a dog' but 'a greyhound'. One accurate adjective beats a stack of near-synonyms — 'the tall, huge, enormous tower' says less than 'the sheer tower'. A useful drafting habit: write the plain version first, then ask of every word — is this the most precise choice, or just the first one that came to mind? Common pitfall: describing everything at the same intensity. Precision also means economy — lavish detail on the object that matters to the scene and sketch the rest, or you slow the story to a crawl. Exam tip: in descriptive tasks, examiners reward controlled, deliberate word choice far more than the number of techniques you squeeze in.

notes.heading: Fresh Comparisons: Using Figurative Language Deliberately
notes.body: You already know simile, metaphor and personification as a reader (see Figurative Language & Literary Devices, eng-figurative-1); as a writer your job is to invent ones nobody has read before. Comparisons like 'as busy as a bee' or 'he slept like a log' are clichés — so overused they slide past the reader's eye without creating any picture. Test every comparison: does it surprise, and does it FIT the mood of the scene? 'The frost furred the window like mould on bread' works in an unsettling scene; it would wreck a cosy one. For extra depth, sustain one comparison into an extended metaphor — if the sea is 'a hungry animal' in sentence one, let it 'prowl', 'bare its teeth' and 'swallow the pier' as the paragraph continues. Allusion is another shortcut: calling a weakness 'her Achilles' heel' packs a whole story into two words — but only if your reader knows the reference, so judge your audience. Common pitfall: device-stacking. One striking image per paragraph outguns five muddled ones, and mixing metaphors ('he drowned in a sea of burning flames') just confuses.

notes.heading: Writing with Sound: Alliteration, Assonance, Consonance and Sibilance
notes.body: Sound patterns let you tune the mood of a sentence the way a film uses music. Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds ('dark, dangerous days'); assonance repeats vowel sounds inside words ('the low moan of the cold stone'); consonance repeats consonant sounds anywhere in nearby words ('the black rocks cracked and clicked'); sibilance repeats hissing s, sh and z sounds, which can feel sinister ('the snake slid silently through the grass') or soothing, depending on context. Onomatopoeia — words that imitate sounds, like 'rattled' or 'hissed' — adds another layer and often carries consonance of its own. The craft lies in matching sound to meaning: soft liquid sounds (l, m, w) slow a scene down and calm it; hard plosives (b, d, k, t) make it harsh and abrupt. Common pitfall: accidental alliteration. If three stressed words in a row happen to start with 'p', readers notice the pattern instead of the meaning — so read your drafts aloud; your ear catches what your eye misses. Use sound deliberately at moments of emphasis rather than wallpapering every sentence with it.

notes.heading: Sentence Length: Controlling the Pace
notes.body: Sentence length is your throttle. Long, multi-clause sentences slow the reader down, which makes them ideal for building dread — detail piles on detail and the tension tightens while the reader waits for the full stop: 'She edged along the corridor, one hand trailing the damp wall, counting every door, telling herself the noises were only pipes, only the wind, only the house settling.' Short sentences do the opposite. They hit. They shock. They make the reader race — which is why 'Help!' feels urgent and 'I would be most grateful if you could assist me' does not. The most powerful pattern combines the two: a long, winding sentence that lulls the reader, then a short one that lands like a punch — the contrast is what creates the impact. Questions in quick succession ('Had they gone? Was it safe?') mimic a panicked mind. Common pitfall: choosing a length by habit rather than by effect — no sentence length is 'good' on its own. Exam tip: when revising a tense scene, deliberately vary lengths; examiners specifically credit controlled sentence variety in narrative and descriptive tasks.

notes.heading: Fragments, One-Word Paragraphs and Dramatic Pauses
notes.body: In fiction you are allowed — sometimes encouraged — to break grammar rules for effect. A fragment is a sentence missing a subject or verb ('No sound. Nothing.'), and a one-word sentence given its own paragraph is more dramatic still; isolating 'Gone.' on its own line forces the reader to stop and stare at it. You can even fracture a complete sentence into one-word sentences: 'The door opened' is information, but 'The. Door. Opened.' makes the reader stress every word, slowing a fast moment into slow motion. Sentence types give you similar control: a simple sentence ('Bony fingers reached for her') is blunt and sinister; joining clauses with 'and' layers on horror, and swapping 'and' for a semicolon delivers the extra detail even faster. Common pitfalls: fragments in essays, reports and formal letters read as errors, so keep this technique for fiction — and inside fiction, ration it. A page full of fragments has no contrast left, and contrast is where the power comes from. Save your shortest sentences and loneliest paragraphs for the story's climactic beats.

notes.heading: Structuring a Narrative for Effect
notes.body: Narrative Techniques & Storytelling (eng-narrative-1) taught you to name structural choices in other people's fiction; now make them yourself. The key planning question is not just 'what happens?' but 'in what order does the reader find out?' A linear structure runs A to Z; a non-linear structure might open with the aftermath — a detective standing over a broken window — then flash back to show how it happened, so readers assemble the puzzle themselves. A flashback delivers backstory at the exact moment it changes how we read the present; a flash-forward (prolepsis) shows a glimpse of what's coming and poisons the present with dread. Foreshadowing plants quiet clues early — a cracked photo frame, an offhand remark — that pay off later and reward attentive readers. Withholding information is a structure too: mystery is simply the gap between what the reader knows and what a character knows. You can also shift focus like a camera, zooming from a whole stormy city down to one lit window, one trembling hand. Common pitfall: non-linear tricks for their own sake confuse readers — signal every time shift clearly and make each reordering earn its place.

notes.heading: Choosing a Narrative Voice: First, Third and Second Person
notes.body: Point of view decides what readers can know and how close they feel, so choose it before you draft. First person ('I', 'we') puts readers inside a character's head: intimate, immediate, and ideal for a distinctive voice — but the narrator can only report what they see, hear and believe, which is perfect for mystery and suspense. That limitation is also a tool: a first-person narrator who lies, exaggerates or misunderstands becomes an unreliable narrator, and readers enjoy spotting the gap between the story they're told and the truth they suspect; a reliable narrator, by contrast, can be trusted. Third person ('he', 'she', 'they') watches from outside: the omniscient version ranges freely across every character's thoughts, while third-person limited follows one character closely but keeps a little distance. Second person ('you') is rare — it drags the reader into the action ('You turn the corner. You freeze.') but is hard to sustain beyond short passages. Common pitfall: head-hopping — drifting between characters' thoughts mid-scene without signalling it. Tip: draft a page of your story in both first and third person and compare; the right choice usually announces itself.

flashcards.definition: A single comparison sustained across several sentences or a whole passage, with every new detail developing the same central image.
flashcards.example: The sea is introduced as 'a hungry animal', then it 'prowls the bay', 'bares its teeth' and 'swallows the pier'.

flashcards.definition: The repetition of vowel sounds within nearby words, used to create mood — often mournful, slow or dreamlike.
flashcards.example: 'The low moan of the cold stone' — the repeated long 'o' sounds make the line feel heavy and sad.

flashcards.definition: The repetition of consonant sounds anywhere in nearby words (not just at the start), adding texture and mood.
flashcards.example: 'The black rocks cracked and clicked' — the repeated hard 'ck' sounds echo the noise being described.

flashcards.definition: A group of words without a full subject–verb structure, used deliberately in fiction for impact or emphasis.
flashcards.example: 'No sound. Nothing.' — fragments that make the silence feel total.

flashcards.definition: The speed at which a story or scene moves, controlled by sentence length, paragraph length and how much detail is given.
flashcards.example: Long descriptive sentences slow the build-up; a burst of short sentences makes a chase feel breathless.

flashcards.definition: Moving the narrative 'camera' deliberately — from a wide view of a scene down to one small, significant detail, or back out.
flashcards.example: From the storm-lashed city, to one lit window, to the trembling hand closing the curtains.

flashcards.definition: A jump ahead in time that shows the reader a glimpse of a future event, creating anticipation or dread.
flashcards.example: 'Years later she would understand what the letter meant — but that night she burned it.'

flashcards.definition: A structure where events are not told in time order — using flashbacks, flash-forwards or reordered scenes so readers piece the story together.
flashcards.example: Opening with the trial's verdict, then flashing back to the night of the crime.

flashcards.definition: Narration using 'he/she/they' that follows one character closely, sharing only what that character knows and feels.
flashcards.example: 'Marcus scanned the empty platform. Where was the train? Something was wrong.'

flashcards.definition: Narration that addresses the reader as 'you', placing them inside the action; immersive but hard to sustain, so rare in fiction.
flashcards.example: 'You turn the corner. You freeze. The footsteps stop too.'

flashcards.definition: A narrator whose version of events the reader can trust — the opposite of an unreliable narrator, who may lie, exaggerate or misunderstand.
flashcards.example: A straightforward witness account the story never contradicts, versus a narrator insisting 'everyone else was to blame'.

flashcards.definition: Deliberately keeping facts from the reader (or from a character) to create mystery and suspense, then revealing them at the most effective moment.
flashcards.example: The narrator mentions 'what happened at the lake' repeatedly but only explains it in the final chapter.

choices: A grammatical error that must never appear in any writing
A very long sentence with several clauses
A group of words missing a subject or verb, used deliberately in fiction for impact
A sentence that contains two independent clauses
questions.explanation: A fragment ('No sound. Nothing.') lacks a full subject–verb structure. In fiction it is a deliberate technique for emphasis — it is not automatically an error, though it would be inappropriate in formal essays. Two independent clauses make a compound sentence, and length has nothing to do with it.

questions.stem: First-person narration is recognised by the use of which pronouns?
choices: 'I' and 'we'
'he', 'she' and 'they'
'you'
'one' and 'it'
questions.explanation: First person means a character narrates their own story using 'I' or 'we', giving intimacy but limiting the reader to what that character knows. 'He/she/they' signal third person, and 'you' signals the rare second person.

choices: the repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby words
the repetition of hissing 's' sounds
words that imitate the sound they describe
the repetition of vowel sounds within nearby words
questions.explanation: Assonance repeats vowel sounds inside words — 'the low moan of the cold stone'. Repeated initial consonants are alliteration, hissing 's' sounds are sibilance, and sound-imitating words are onomatopoeia. All four are sound devices, so keep the definitions distinct.

questions.stem: In narrative structure, a flashback is:
choices: a subtle hint planted early about events still to come
a scene that takes the reader back to an earlier event
a glimpse shown of a future event
a fast-paced action sequence
questions.explanation: A flashback interrupts the present timeline to show something that happened earlier, usually delivering backstory at the moment it matters most. A hint about the future is foreshadowing, a glimpse of the future is a flash-forward, and pace is unrelated to the definition.

questions.stem: In a tense scene, a burst of short sentences usually makes the pace feel:
choices: slower and more reflective
unchanged — only word choice affects pace
faster and more urgent
confusing and hard to follow
questions.explanation: Short sentences are quick to read, so the reader races through them — which is why 'Help!' feels more urgent than a polite, long request. Long sentences slow the pace for build-up; the contrast between the two is what creates impact.

questions.stem: Which revision of 'The boy went into the dark room' is the strongest example of word-level precision?
choices: 'The boy went quickly and nervously into the dark room.'
'The boy crept into the unlit room.'
'The boy went into the dark, gloomy, shadowy room.'
'The dark room was entered by the boy.'
questions.explanation: 'Crept' replaces both 'went' and the adverbs 'quickly and nervously' — one precise verb does the work of three vague words, and 'unlit' is sharper than stacked synonyms like 'dark, gloomy, shadowy'. The passive version ('was entered by') drains the sentence of energy without adding precision.

questions.stem: Which line uses sound devices most effectively to create a sinister mood?
choices: 'The puppy bounced briskly behind the bench.'
'She sang sweet songs at sunrise.'
'The cat crept carefully across the carpet.'
'The snake slid silently through the wet, whispering grass.'
questions.explanation: The hissing sibilance of 'snake slid silently... whispering grass' matches sound to a sinister meaning. The other lines contain alliteration too, but their sounds suit cheerful or gentle scenes — a device only creates the intended effect when its sound fits the mood you want.

questions.stem: A writer wants readers to gradually suspect that the person telling the story may be lying about what happened. Which narrative choice best achieves this?
choices: A first-person unreliable narrator, so readers only receive the narrator's biased version
A third-person omniscient narrator who confirms the truth of every event
Second-person narration addressing the reader as 'you'
A reliable first-person narrator who reports events accurately
questions.explanation: First person locks readers inside one character's account; if that account is inconsistent or self-serving, readers start reading between the lines — the effect the writer wants. An omniscient narrator or a reliable narrator would close down the suspicion, and second person says nothing about truthfulness.

questions.stem: Why might a writer use one long, multi-clause sentence in the middle of a suspenseful scene?
choices: Because examiners require at least one long sentence per paragraph
To make the action feel faster and more chaotic
To slow the pace and let tension build as detail accumulates
To signal that a character is about to speak
questions.explanation: Long sentences hold the reader inside a single unfolding moment — detail piles up and the full stop is delayed, tightening suspense. Short sentences create speed and shock, not long ones; there is no quota rule, and sentence length has no link to introducing speech.

questions.stem: Which of these stories has a non-linear structure?
choices: A story told in strict time order from the hero's birth to old age
A story that opens with the trial's verdict, then flashes back to the night of the crime
A diary written day by day across one school term
A journey story where each chapter covers the next stage of the trip
questions.explanation: Opening with the outcome and then flashing back reorders time, so readers assemble events themselves — that is non-linear structure. The other options all present events in chronological order, which is the definition of a linear narrative.

questions.stem: Which passage contains an extended metaphor?
choices: 'The exam hall was as quiet as a library.'
'The old house groaned in the wind.'
'He was as busy as a bee all morning.'
'Doubt crept into her mind. It built a nest there, laid its eggs, and soon every thought hatched into worry.'
questions.explanation: An extended metaphor sustains one comparison across several sentences — here doubt becomes a nesting bird and every new detail develops that same image. 'As quiet as a library' is a single simile, 'groaned' is a brief personification, and 'busy as a bee' is a clichéd simile, not an extended one.

questions.stem: Read this passage: 'The fog came down slowly over the town, muffling the streets, softening every edge, until the whole place seemed to hold its breath. Then the siren. One long note.' Which best describes the writer's craft?
choices: Alliteration is used throughout to create a humorous tone
A flashback reveals what happened before the fog arrived
Personification and a shift from long to short sentences turn calm into shock
An omniscient narrator explains what every character is thinking
questions.explanation: The town 'seemed to hold its breath' (personification) builds unease across one long, winding sentence; the fragment 'Then the siren. One long note.' then jolts the reader — the long-to-short contrast is the engine of the effect. There is no humour, no flashback, and no access to any character's thoughts.

questions.stem: A writer wants a comparison that feels fresh AND fits a bleak, decaying mood. Which line succeeds on both counts?
choices: 'The frost furred the window like mould spreading over bread.'
'Her hands were as cold as ice.'
'The garden was as dead as a doornail.'
'The ruined factory loomed like a giant birthday cake.'
questions.explanation: Frost compared to spreading mould is original and its decaying image reinforces the bleak mood. 'Cold as ice' and 'dead as a doornail' are clichés — fresh-sounding is not enough, though: the birthday-cake image is original but clashes comically with the ruined, bleak setting.

questions.stem: A writer wants readers to feel growing unease about a character's mysterious past without revealing it too soon. Which structural strategy works best?
choices: Explain the character's entire backstory in the opening paragraph so readers feel informed
Have an omniscient narrator state the secret plainly in chapter one
Avoid mentioning the past at all until the final line, so it comes from nowhere
Withhold the backstory, drop small hints through the story, then reveal it in a late flashback
questions.explanation: Withholding information creates the gap between what readers know and suspect; planted hints feed the unease, and a late flashback pays it off at the moment of maximum impact. Revealing everything early kills the mystery, while withholding every hint until the last line makes the reveal feel unearned rather than suspenseful.

questions.stem: Why does 'The. Door. Opened.' feel more dramatic than 'The door opened.'?
choices: It corrects a grammatical error in the original sentence
Breaking it into one-word sentences forces the reader to stress each word, slowing the moment down for emphasis
It speeds up the pace of the scene
It adds extra information about the door
questions.explanation: Fracturing the sentence isolates each word, so the reader lingers on every beat — a fast event is stretched into slow motion, which heightens the drama. The original was already grammatical, the effect slows rather than speeds the pace, and no new information is added.
